questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that network- and identity-layer zero trust controls alone are not enough to protect sensitive data?
options: Because once access is legitimately granted, the data itself carries no memory of that decision as it moves beyond the original boundary
Because sensitivity labels replace the need for any network segmentation at all
Because DLP can only inspect email traffic and nothing else
Because encryption at rest is impossible once a file is stored in the cloud
questions.explain: Network and identity controls govern the access decision at a boundary. Once data is legitimately released, it carries no trace of that decision — protection has to move onto the asset itself via classification, encryption, and DLP.

questions.q: What makes a sensitivity label useful as a zero-trust control rather than just a visual marker?
options: It permanently deletes the file after a fixed retention period
It replaces the need for TLS encryption in transit
It is machine-readable metadata that downstream systems (mail gateways, cloud apps, DLP engines) act on automatically
It only matters for files stored on removable media
questions.explain: A label is only effective once systems downstream can read it and enforce policy against it — blocking external forwarding, blocking public sharing, or flagging risky copies — not just displaying it to a human.

questions.q: How does rights-management-style encryption differ from simply encrypting data at rest in a storage account?
options: It only applies to data stored on-premises, never in the cloud
It removes the need for a managed key service like Key Vault or KMS
It is identical — there is no practical difference between the two
It binds the decryption key to an access policy rather than a location, so the content stays protected even after it leaves the originating network
questions.explain: Rights-management encryption evaluates policy and identity conditions at the moment of decryption, wherever that happens, instead of only protecting data while it sits inside storage you control.

questions.q: What is confidential computing, as described in this lesson?
options: A legal agreement that restricts who can view a classification policy document
Hardware-backed techniques that keep data encrypted even while it is being processed in memory, sometimes called encryption in use
A synonym for encrypting data only while it is in transit over TLS
A DLP rule that blocks printing of confidential files
questions.explain: Confidential computing extends encryption into the processing stage itself, so even a compromised host or hypervisor cannot read the data while it is being used.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say a DLP program that only inspects the email gateway is incomplete?
options: Because DLP policies cannot be applied to email at all
Because email is never actually a channel for data loss
Because sensitive content can leave through other channels too — endpoint file copies, browser uploads to cloud apps, printing, removable media — and those need the same policy enforcement
Because DLP policies should only be based on sensitivity labels, never on content pattern matching
questions.explain: The zero-trust property of DLP is consistent enforcement across every channel data could travel through. Watching one chokepoint while leaving others uninspected leaves the asset unprotected on those other paths.
